efe7d2f7351d22d406e3117d510c62b8f556ed34.summary: A Medium blog post by Wade Hickey, published 2022-03-05, describing how the author recovered the password of a leaked Conti ransomware source code archive. One leaked archive was posted without a password, and known plaintext from it was used with the bkcrack tool to crack the password-protected one. The post names the Conti ransomware group and lists three archive file names, but gives no sector, country, or attribution detail.

Targets include Korean universities, national defense and other companies. Initial access used Innorix Agent abuse and likely spear phishing. Malware includes Go-based backdoors such as Goat RAT and DurianBeacon, plus AndarLoader. The report says the initial distribution route is unconfirmed and that the link to past Andariel cases is inferred, not direct.

ef7db37bc011fea9853410fdc8938b9a0b789300.summary: Jamf Threat Labs reports DPRK-linked social engineering against crypto-industry individuals, after an FBI warning. Attacks start with a fake recruiter on a professional networking platform, then a zipped coding challenge that runs commands on build and drops Thiefbucket (also called Rustdoor), a backdoor and infostealer. Variants persist via cron or the zshrc file, and one prompts for a password styled as Visual Studio. Jamf ties the malware to DPRK activity via its delivery methods.

ef1a1866916d19c941f558a4426fdc1d3f56a30a.summary: Microsoft analyses XorDdos, a Linux trojan that spreads mainly through SSH brute-force attacks and builds botnets for DDoS attacks. It uses daemon processes, XOR-encoded strings, process name spoofing, an optional kernel rootkit and cron/init persistence to stay hidden. The report says activity rose 254% over six months and that devices infected with XorDdos were later infected with the Tsunami backdoor and the XMRig coin miner.
